flowchart TD
    %% Windows Interaction Layer
    WinExplorer["Windows Explorer/Net Use"]:::windows
    SSHFSWrapper["SSHFS-Win Wrapper (sshfs-win.c)"]:::windows

    %% POSIX Integration Layer
    subgraph "POSIX Layer"
        Cygwin["Cygwin Environment"]:::posix
        SSHFSEngine["Patched SSHFS Engine (Submodule+Patches)"]:::posix
        Cygwin -->|"runs"| SSHFSEngine
    end

    %% External and Windows Filesystem Integration
    RemoteSSH["Remote SSH Host (SSH)"]:::posix
    WinFsp["WinFsp (FUSE for Windows)"]:::windows

    %% Build & Deployment Layer
    subgraph "Build & Deployment"
        BuildProcess["Build Process (Makefile)"]:::build
        InstallerConfig["Installer Configuration (sshfs-win.wxs)"]:::build
        PatchIntegration["Patch Integration (patches)"]:::build
        ArtResources["Art Resources (art)"]:::build
        EtcFiles["Configuration Files (etc)"]:::build
    end

    %% Flow of operations
    WinExplorer -->|"initiates"| SSHFSWrapper
    SSHFSWrapper -->|"calls"| Cygwin
    SSHFSEngine -->|"sends_ops"| WinFsp
    SSHFSEngine -->|"communicates"| RemoteSSH
    WinFsp -->|"mounts_drive"| WinExplorer

    %% Build Process Flow
    BuildProcess -->|"packages_into"| InstallerConfig
    PatchIntegration -->|"integrated_into"| InstallerConfig
    ArtResources -->|"integrated_into"| InstallerConfig
    EtcFiles -->|"integrated_into"| InstallerConfig
    InstallerConfig -->|"deploys"| SSHFSWrapper

<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README, this project is a Windows port of SSHFS—it enables you to map a remote SSH filesystem as a network drive on Windows. The project cleverly integrates the upstream SSHFS (included as a submodule) with a Windows‐friendly wrapper (sshfs-win.c) and installer configuration (sshfs-win.wxs) so that it works with key components such as Cygwin (providing a POSIX environment) and WinFsp (providing the FUSE functionality). Here’s how to approach drawing the best and most accurate system design diagram for this project:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Windows Shell/Explorer & Networking: Represent how the user or the “net use” command interacts with the mapped network drive.
   • SSHFS-Win Wrapper: The sshfs-win.c file is the main entry point; it acts as a wrapper to translate Windows drive mapping requests into calls to SSHFS.
   • Upstream SSHFS Submodule: Highlight that the project includes the full SSHFS code (patched by files in the “patches” directory) to do the heavy lifting.
   • Cygwin Environment: Illustrate that a POSIX-like environment (provided by Cygwin) is required to run the SSHFS binary.
   • WinFsp (and its related components): Indicate that WinFsp provides the FUSE (Filesystem in Userspace) functionality on Windows so that the mounted filesystem appears native.
   • Build and Installer Components: Include the Makefile, Wix installer file (sshfs-win.wxs), and additional tools (such as registry patch files in “etc” and “patches”) as part of the build/packaging process.

2. Show Relationships and Data Flow:
   • Begin the diagram with the Windows user interacting with the mapped drive (via Windows Explorer or command line “net use”). Use an arrow to show a call into the SSHFS-Win wrapper (sshfs-win.c).
   • From the wrapper, depict a call into the patched SSHFS core (managed as a submodule), which runs in a Cygwin environment.
   • Show that the SSHFS process communicates with the remote SSHFS host over SSH (including options for tunneling or key-based authentication as explained in the README).
   • Illustrate interaction with WinFsp: after the SSHFS/Cygwin layer decodes the network drive operations, WinFsp translates them into Windows file system calls.
   • Optionally, add the build and installer components on the side. Show that the build process (driven by the Makefile and patches incorporated from “patches”, “art”, and “etc”) packages everything into an MSI installer via the Wix configuration.

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns:
   • Emphasize the layered architecture: Windows front end (user interactions) → Wrapper & integration layer → POSIX SSHFS engine (with patches) → WinFsp file system integration.
   • Note that the project uses external dependencies (Cygwin for POSIX, WinFsp for FUSE) and patches over upstream SSHFS to meet Windows-specific requirements.
   • The separation of concerns is clear—the wrapper handles Windows connectivity logic and the SSHFS submodule handles remote filesystem semantics.

4. Instructions for the Diagram’s Visual Elements:
   • Clearly label each component (e.g., “Windows Explorer/Net Use”, “SSHFS-Win Wrapper (sshfs-win.c)”, “Patched SSHFS Engine (submodule + patches)”, “Cygwin POSIX Environment”, “WinFsp (FUSE for Windows)”, and “Installer/Build Process”).
   • Use directional arrows to indicate the flow of commands and data:
       - For example, an arrow from “Windows Explorer” to “SSHFS-Win Wrapper”, then from the wrapper to “Cygwin SSHFS Engine”, and from there to “Remote SSH Host” (over SSH).
       - Also, include arrows from the SSHFS engine to WinFsp to highlight file system operations.
   • Employ color coding or different shapes to visually separate Windows-specific components (like the installer and WinFsp) from the POSIX/Cygwin-based parts.
   • Include a side box or label describing the build process (Makefile driving the compilation, submodules initialization, patching, and creation of the MSI installer via WinFsp’s signature tool, Wix file, and registry tweaks).

5. Tailor the Diagram Specifically:
   • Since this is not a full-stack web app or a compiler but a filesystem porting tool, focus your diagram on the integration of the SSHFS functionality into the Windows system.
   • Clearly indicate the external dependencies (Cygwin, WinFsp, and Wix Toolset) and show their roles.
   • The build process is as simple as running Make, initializing the SSHFS submodule, and packaging into an installer; make sure to cover this in a separate “Build & Deployment” section of the diagram.

In summary, your diagram should be detailed and layered. It should capture:
   - The components: Windows shell instance, SSHFS-Win wrapper, patched SSHFS engine running in Cygwin, and the WinFsp integration layer.
   - Their relationships: How a network drive mapping request in Windows is passed through these components culminating in the remote SSH filesystem being available on the Windows file system.
   - The additional build and packaging steps that convert source code to a ready-to-install MSI.

By following these guidelines and labeling each component clearly, you’ll produce a comprehensive system design diagram that accurately represents the architecture of SSHFS-Win and its integration with Windows. Happy diagramming!
</explanation>
